newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada corporate profits climb in 1st quarter.
newsitem.headline: Canada corporate profits climb in 1st quarter.

text.p: Canada's surging domestic economy fueled a healthy gain in corporate profits in the first quarter of 1997, and economists expect the growth to continue for the rest of the year.

"We have the economy operating on more cylinders, the consumers back on line, and that therefore is spilling over into a better profit picture for our durable goods producers," said MMS International economist Rob Palombi.
"This could extend well into the second half of this year," he added.
First-quarter earnings of the 176 companies in Reuters' quarterly survey rose 22.4 percent to C$6.66 billion ($4.8 billion) from the same period a year earlier.
Revenues for the companies, which represent the bulk of the Toronto Stock Exchange's key 300 composite index, rose 11.7 percent to C$115 billion ($82.9 billion) in the same period.
Boosted by low interest rates and increased consumer spending, companies in 11 of the Toronto exchange's 14 subindexes saw a year-over-year increase in quarterly profits.

Consumer products, real estate and construction, transportation and communications all posted triple-digit profit growth, while banks, industrials and merchandising recorded less dramatic but still impressive earnings.
Nesbitt Burns Chief Economist Sherry Cooper said companies geared to the domestic market were reaping the rewards of cost-cutting.

"Labor demands in Canada have been very muted, because the unemployment rate is still so high and there have been so many layoffs and so much restructuring, wage demands will continue to be quite moderate," Cooper said.
She said Canada's economy would continue to grow, albeit at a scaled-down rate, fueling corporate Canada to outperform its U.S. counterpart.
Companies in the consumer products sector earned 334.4 percent more profit in the first quarter than a year ago.
The banking sector reaped further dividends from low interest rates, as profits and revenues climbed 13.8 percent and 10.1 percent, respectively.
Palombi said the outlook for the booming bank sector remained positive as fears of an interest rate hike receded.

"It looks as though we're not going to be seeing any major tightening of policy by the U.S. over the near term, and as a result Canadian interest rates should remain steady. So the outlook for the banking sector is not bearish by any stretch," Palombi said.
Canada's resource sectors marred the otherwise rosy earnings picture, as low commodity prices dragged down profits.

The metals sector saw earnings slip 23.3 percent in the quarter, while golds fell 23.1 percent. Revenues slipped three percent and 1.6 percent, respectively, for the sectors, and economists said the future was clouded.

"Though we've seen a minor increase in gold prices recently, the fact that gold is still below 350 (dollars an ounce) is a negative. We're not forecasting any substantial improvement in that sector over the near term," Cooper said.

Paper and forest products companies were again the hardest hit sector, as commodity prices languished. Earnings for the group fell 120.2 percent, but Cooper said the sector should begin to improve late in the second half of 1997.
"We do think that newsprint will begin to recover, and so the forest products earnings have bottomed," she said.
